The train / test split is a classic camera-trap domain shift with a first-order sensor-modality / acquisition-geometry gap and a second-order optics gap.

Train = GBIF multimedia: daytime visible-light colour RGB, arbitrary cameras, viewpoints, backgrounds, distances, essentially sharp. Deploy = fixed-point night IR trap: 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness near-IR illuminant → effectively spectrally monochrome / R≈G≈B and illumination level essentially constant; one body fixed to the rock face, 50 mm lens, 7 m baseline to opposite rock, focus locked at 3.5 m mid-point, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s, exposure/aperture/ISO fixed for the whole season, background = the two rocks.

Immediate consequences held across rounds:
* Brightness / luminance jitter A,B,C is counter-productive: illuminant and exposure stack are fixed, so global linear / tone-curve brightness injects a nuisance never seen in deployment.
* Colour operations A,B,C,I,J cannot create the colour → IR monochrome modality shift. Deployment frames are R≈G≈B. RGB multiplicative, tone-curve, channel swizzle, colour noise all operate in colour space absent at test time and encourage reliance on chromatic cues spurious in IR.
* Noise J,K and motion blur H are not first order: ISO 190 f/4 1/500 s under constant IR is low noise, high speed; directional motion blur from terrestrial mammals in a pinch point is negligible.
* Scale D is tightly constrained by fixed 7 m geometry; apparent size set by species size and small depth excursion. Flips E,F are unphysical for a fixed rock background; vertical flip impossible and horizontal mirror mirrors fixed rock texture.
* The only systematic optical degradation imposed by the rig is fixed mid-point depth of field. With f=50 mm N=4.0 s0≈3.5 m geometrical DOF is O(1 m), ~3.0–4.2 m for conventional CoC. Whole 7 m ravine is mostly outside in-focus slab, so animals near entrance/exit are systematically defocused whereas GBIF images are essentially sharp. That is a spatial acutance loss, not photometric.

Why G is repeatedly singled out in round 2:
A 11×11 σ≈3 px Gaussian blur is the only listed transform with a direct hardware analogue: it approximates fixed-focus depth-of-field defocus / out-of-focus loss of acutance for subjects off 3.5 m. Colleagues 1,3,5,8 argue this is the least unphysical and only physically motivated proxy among A-K. The train/test mismatch is hardware-written, not generic ImageNet jitter.

Train = GBIF multimedia: daylight visible RGB, essentially sharp, arbitrary camera/background/pose/distance/illumination.
Deploy = one fixed night IR trap: 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise under fixed-brightness near-IR illuminator, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, 50 mm focal length, camera body fixed to a rock face facing the opposite rock 7 m away, focus locked at ~3.5 m mid-ravine, background = two rock faces, framing essentially fixed for the season. Scene is effectively spectrally monochrome / R≈G≈B and photometry is essentially constant by lamp+fixed ISO/f/T.

First-order shifts
* Modality / photometry. At test illumination/exposure/ISO/aperture/shutter are fixed for the season and the data is effectively grey-scale IR. Linear brightness A, linear luminance brightness B, non-linear tone-curve C, RGB channel swizzle I, colour noise J, B/W noise K all operate in RGB colour space. They cannot create a visible → near-IR spectral mapping, cannot remove colour reliance learned from GBIF daylight images, and A,B,C inject brightness jitter never seen at test. Swizzle permutes colour but does not remove colour reliance nor make R≈G≈B statistics.
* Geometry / framing / scale. Apparent size, perspective and background are set by the 7 m pinch point and fixed 50 mm viewpoint. Scale D adds spurious size variance. Vertical flip E is physically impossible and horizontal mirror F mirrors a fixed asymmetric rock texture / fixed framing prior never sampled in the field.
* Noise / motion. 1/500 s at ISO 190 under constant IR lamp is low-noise high-speed. Directional motion blur H and sensor noise J,K are not first order deployment nuisances for terrestrial mammals in a pinch point.

Second-order optics
Fixed mid-point focus imposes systematic depth-of-field loss of acutance. With f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m, geometrical near/far ≈3.0–4.2 m for conventional CoC, ~0.8–1.2 m total in-focus interval. Animals at entrance/exit of the 7 m corridor are systematically defocused w.r.t. mid-plane whereas GBIF images are essentially sharp. Spatial blur is the only transform with a direct physical analogue. Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ≈3 px is the proxy for that fixed-focus / DOF defocus / out-of-focus softness for subjects off the 3.5 m plane.
